answer_unit.question_ref: Specimen Examination Paper 2, Question 5, page 6, parts 5.1 and 5.2(i)-(ii), total 20 marks

regime_entity.value: Offshore asset-holding company; British Virgin Islands business company for part 5.2(i)

legal_actor_capacity.value: Company distributing to shareholders; directors authorising a distribution; beneficial owner funding the company; administrators structuring the initial funding

transaction_relationship.value: Company-member distribution and company-beneficial-owner debtor-creditor funding relationship

lifecycle_stage.value: Capital initially introduced, followed by later return of assets by distribution or repayment

governing_instruments.value: Common-law capital-maintenance rule in Re Flitcroft's Case (1882) and the British Virgin Islands Business Companies Act 2004 distribution regime; no actual memorandum or articles supplied

facts.text: The company is an offshore money-box company whose function is to hold assets.

facts.value: flexible lawful return of assets to shareholders
facts.text: The company must be able lawfully to distribute corporate assets to shareholders flexibly at the time and in the amount required by the beneficial owner.
Part 5.1 commands a review of the common-law rule in Re Flitcroft's Case (1882), often codified by companies legislation, and a description of its rationale.
Part 5.1 also asks to what extent the objectives of the rule were achieved in practice.
Part 5.2 asks how the rules in Re Flitcroft's Case are circumvented or avoided.
For part 5.2(i), the candidate must choose a jurisdiction, state it clearly in a preliminary paragraph and apply it consistently throughout.
Part 5.2(i) asks how companies legislation in the chosen jurisdiction avoids the common-law restriction.
Part 5.2(ii) asks about corporate practice adopted by administrators when establishing the financial structure of an offshore company when capital is initially introduced.
Part 5.2 carries 10 marks across sub-parts (i) and (ii), and Question 5 carries 20 marks in total.

claims.text: The common-law capital-maintenance rule restricts distributions from capital and must be distinguished from distributions of profit.
The rule's creditor-protection rationale and its practical effectiveness require separate treatment.
The British Virgin Islands statutory distribution regime replaces capital maintenance with a solvency-based authorisation route.
Administrators can place only a nominal amount into share capital and introduce the balance as shareholder debt, allowing later repayment in the creditor capacity.

routes.unique_contribution: Capital-account distinctions, the Re Flitcroft rule and rationale, practical limits of capital maintenance, the British Virgin Islands solvency-distribution model and the nominal-capital/shareholder-loan practice.
The corporate decision procedure for a British Virgin Islands distribution, including board authorisation, solvency assessment and the role of the memorandum and articles.
The operative distribution-resolution precedent is excluded because Question 5 asks for prose analysis, not a drafted resolution.
The traditional board-recommendation dividend precedent is a wrong-regime drafting route for the selected British Virgin Islands prose answer.
The traditional member-declaration dividend precedent is a wrong-regime drafting route for the selected British Virgin Islands prose answer.
The alternative traditional board-only dividend precedent is excluded because it does not supply the selected British Virgin Islands solvency-distribution regime and no drafting is requested.
Insolvency, recovery and creditor-priority consequences are background only because the question supplies no insolvency, winding-up or enforcement event.
